slides: Welcome back. Now a tool for necessarily-true questions with letters. I call it the mirror test, and it can cross out choices without solving anything.

slides.say: Look at the given, and change it in one of two ways. One, flip every sign, so x becomes minus x, and y becomes minus y. Two, swap the letters, so x becomes y, and y becomes x.
If the given looks exactly the same after the change, the given is a mirror. And why does that help? Because any numbers that fit the given, their mirror fits it too.
Let's see it in numbers. Say the swap keeps the given the same, and x two, y nine fit it. Then x nine, y two fit it too.

Now look at a choice. If the mirror turns it into its opposite, it can't always be true. Take x smaller than y. Two and nine say yes. Their mirror, nine and two, says no. So it's not necessarily true, and we cross it out.
So when do you reach for it? A necessarily question, letters, and a given that looks balanced.

Let's try one. Given, the absolute value of a plus b is smaller than the absolute value of a plus the absolute value of b. Which of these is necessarily negative? a, b minus a, a times b, or a plus b.

First, is the given a mirror? Flip all signs. Minus a minus b has the same absolute value as a plus b. And minus a and minus b have the same sizes as a and b. So the given doesn't change, it's a mirror.
Now a turns into minus a. If a were always negative, minus a would have to be always negative too. But they're opposites, so both can't hold. Out.
b minus a turns into a minus b, and a plus b turns into minus a minus b. Each one turns into its opposite, so they're out too.
And a times b? Minus a times minus b is a times b. It doesn't change. It's the only one left, so that's the answer.
A quick check. a two and b negative one. Two minus one is one, and one is smaller than two plus one, three. And a times b is negative two. Negative.
at: a two and b negative one

slides.say: Here's one where both mirrors work. Given, x squared plus y squared is thirteen. Which is necessarily true? x is positive, x is smaller than y, x plus y is positive, or x squared is at most thirteen.
Flip the signs. Minus x, squared, is x squared, so the given doesn't change. x positive turns into x negative, and x plus y positive turns into x plus y negative. Both out.
Now swap. y squared plus x squared is thirteen, the same given again. x smaller than y turns into y smaller than x. Opposites, so it's out.
One choice is left, x squared is at most thirteen. And it's true, because y squared is never negative, so x squared can't pass thirteen.
Now careful here. In the swap, it turns into y squared at most thirteen. That's a twin, not an opposite. Twins stay, only opposites go out.
[short pause] Now three limits. First, always check the given. If the swap changes it, like a plus b in bars bigger than two b, which turns into bigger than two a, there's no mirror and no test.
Second, simplify a choice before you mirror it. x minus y plus two y looks lopsided, but it's just x plus y.
Third, if every choice survives the mirror, the test doesn't help. Then go back to plugging in numbers.
So the rule is, if the given doesn't change in the mirror, a choice that turns into its opposite is not necessarily true. [pause] Try it on the next question. Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
